questions.prompt: A technician runs the command on a Windows laptop. Which statement correctly explains the output?
options: Two separate WLANs happen to use the same name, and the client must choose one by typing its BSSID
The access point is misconfigured, because each radio in an AP must advertise a different SSID
One SSID is served by two radios of one AP, and each radio's cell is identified by its own BSSID
The 2.4 GHz entry is a rogue access point, because its MAC address differs from the 5 GHz entry
questions.explanation: The SSID is the WLAN's name; the **BSSID** is the MAC address of one radio's cell. A dual-band AP has a 2.4 GHz radio and a 5 GHz radio, each with its own BSSID, and both advertise the same SSID. The two BSSIDs differing only in the last digit is typical of one AP deriving addresses from its base MAC.

whyWrong.0: One SSID with several BSSIDs is normal; the client picks a BSSID itself and the user never types one.
whyWrong.1: Advertising one SSID from both radios is the standard dual-band design, not a misconfiguration.
whyWrong.3: Different radios always have different BSSIDs; two consecutive MACs point to the same AP, not a rogue.

questions.prompt: An access point transmits at 20 dBm. The administrator raises the transmit power by 3 dB. What is the new transmit power in milliwatts?
options: 50 mW
200 mW
400 mW
questions.explanation: 20 dBm is 100 mW (0 dBm = 1 mW, and each +10 dB multiplies by 10). Adding 3 dB doubles the power, so 23 dBm is 200 mW.

whyWrong.0: 50 mW would be 17 dBm — a 3 dB *decrease*.
whyWrong.2: 400 mW is 26 dBm, which would need +6 dB (two doublings).
whyWrong.3: 1,000 mW is 30 dBm, a +10 dB change, not +3 dB.

questions.prompt: A client measures a received signal of −65 dBm while the noise floor is −92 dBm. What is the signal-to-noise ratio?
options: 27 dB
−157 dBm
27 dBm
−27 dB
questions.explanation: SNR is the signal level minus the noise level: −65 − (−92) = 27. Because it is a difference between two dBm values it is a ratio, expressed in **dB**.

whyWrong.1: Adding the two levels is meaningless; SNR is a subtraction, and the result is never in dBm.
whyWrong.2: The arithmetic is right but the unit is wrong: a ratio between two powers is in dB, not dBm.
whyWrong.3: SNR is signal minus noise, so a signal above the noise floor gives a positive number.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about the 2.4 GHz band are true? (Choose two.)
options: Bonding two channels into a 40 MHz channel doubles the number of non-overlapping channels available
Channel centres are 5 MHz apart, but each transmission is 20–22 MHz wide, so neighbouring channel numbers overlap
Channels 1, 2 and 3 provide three independent channels because they have different channel numbers
Only channels 1, 6 and 11 are far enough apart (25 MHz) not to overlap in the North American plan
Channels 12 and 13 require DFS because they share spectrum with weather radar
questions.explanation: The 2.4 GHz channels are numbered every 5 MHz but a 20 MHz (802.11b: 22 MHz) transmission covers four channel steps on either side, so only channels whose centres are 25 MHz apart — 1, 6 and 11 — are clean of each other.

whyWrong.0: A 40 MHz channel consumes nearly half the band and *reduces* the usable channels to one or two.
whyWrong.2: Channels 1, 2 and 3 overlap almost completely; a different number does not mean a different frequency range.
whyWrong.4: DFS applies only to the 5 GHz channels 52–64 and 100–144; no 2.4 GHz channel requires a radar check.

questions.prompt: AP-C was just installed at the end of the corridor, within range of AP-B. Users near AP-B and AP-C now report Wi-Fi that is slow but error-free. What is happening, and what should change?
options: Adjacent-channel interference between AP-B and AP-C; move AP-C to channel 8
Co-channel interference between AP-A and AP-C; move AP-A to channel 6
Adjacent-channel interference between AP-A and AP-B; move AP-B to channel 3
Co-channel interference between AP-B and AP-C; move AP-C to channel 11
questions.explanation: AP-B and AP-C both use channel 6 within range of each other, so CSMA/CA makes the two cells take turns: throughput drops but frames are not corrupted, the classic **co-channel** symptom. Channel 11 is the only remaining non-overlapping channel next to a channel-6 cell.

whyWrong.0: Same channel means co-channel, not adjacent-channel; and channel 8 would overlap both 6 and 11, making it worse.
whyWrong.1: AP-A is on channel 1, two cells away from AP-C; they neither share nor overlap a channel.
whyWrong.2: Channels 1 and 6 do not overlap, and channel 3 would overlap both 1 and 6.

questions.prompt: On which 5 GHz channels must an access point listen for radar for 60 seconds before it may transmit?
options: 36–48 only
Every channel above 36
questions.explanation: Channels 52–64 (UNII-2A) and 100–144 (UNII-2C) share spectrum with radar, so they require **Dynamic Frequency Selection**: a 60-second channel availability check, leaving within 10 seconds if radar appears, and 30 minutes of non-occupancy.

whyWrong.1: UNII-1 (36–48) has no radar users and no DFS requirement.
whyWrong.2: UNII-3 (149–165) is DFS-free; it is the other block used when DFS must be avoided.
whyWrong.3: Channels 40–48 and 149–165 are above 36, yet none of them requires DFS.

questions.prompt: Which 802.11 amendment operates only in the 5 GHz band and introduced 80 MHz channels and 256-QAM?
questions.explanation: **802.11ac** (Wi-Fi 5) is 5 GHz only; it added 80 and 160 MHz channels, 256-QAM and downlink MU-MIMO for a 6.9 Gbps maximum.

whyWrong.0: 802.11n works in both bands and stops at 40 MHz channels and 64-QAM.
whyWrong.2: 802.11ax runs in 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz and uses 1024-QAM; it inherited 80 MHz from ac.
whyWrong.3: 802.11g is a 2.4 GHz, 54 Mbps, 20 MHz standard.

questions.prompt: Which was the first 802.11 amendment able to operate in the 6 GHz band?
options: 802.11ac Wave 2
questions.explanation: **802.11ax** devices certified for 6 GHz are marketed as Wi-Fi 6E; the band was opened in 2020 and only ax and the later 802.11be may use it.

whyWrong.0: 802.11ac, including Wave 2, is a 5 GHz-only standard.
whyWrong.1: 802.11n covers 2.4 and 5 GHz only.
whyWrong.2: 802.11a is the original 5 GHz OFDM standard from 1999.

questions.prompt: Which two features distinguish WPA3-Personal from WPA2-Personal? (Choose two.)
options: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) replaces the pre-shared key exchange
TKIP replaces CCMP as the mandatory cipher
Protected management frames (802.11w) are mandatory
A RADIUS server is required to validate the passphrase
The passphrase must be at least 64 characters long
questions.explanation: WPA3-Personal authenticates with **SAE**, which resists offline dictionary attacks and gives forward secrecy, and it requires **PMF** so that de-authentication frames cannot be spoofed. The cipher stays AES-CCMP.

whyWrong.1: TKIP is the deprecated WPA cipher; WPA3 forbids it and keeps CCMP (GCMP-256 in Enterprise 192-bit mode).
whyWrong.3: RADIUS belongs to Enterprise mode; Personal mode still uses a passphrase, just with a better exchange.
whyWrong.4: The passphrase rules are unchanged: 8 to 63 characters.

questions.prompt: Based on the output, which statement about this wireless connection is accurate?
options: The client authenticated with 802.1X and an EAP method against a RADIUS server
Channel 44 is a DFS channel, so the AP performed a radar check before serving it
Frames are encrypted with AES-CCMP using keys derived from a shared passphrase
TKIP is in use, because WPA2-Personal always negotiates RC4-based encryption
questions.explanation: `WPA2-Personal` means a pre-shared passphrase, and `Cipher: CCMP` means AES in counter mode with CBC-MAC — the secure WPA2 combination.

whyWrong.0: 802.1X/EAP would show as WPA2-Enterprise.
whyWrong.1: Channel 44 is in UNII-1 (36–48), which has no DFS requirement; DFS starts at channel 52.
whyWrong.3: The Cipher line says CCMP; TKIP is optional in WPA2 and clearly not negotiated here.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of a wireless security certification with its cipher is correct?
options: WPA2 — AES-CCMP
WEP — TKIP
WPA — AES-GCMP
WPA3 — RC4
questions.explanation: WPA2 implemented IEEE 802.11i with **AES-CCMP**. The full ladder is WEP → RC4, WPA → TKIP (RC4 with per-packet keys), WPA2 → AES-CCMP, WPA3 → AES-CCMP or GCMP-256.

whyWrong.1: WEP uses plain RC4 with a static key; TKIP was WPA's fix for it.
whyWrong.2: WPA uses TKIP; GCMP arrived with WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode.
whyWrong.3: WPA3 never uses RC4 in any form.

questions.prompt: Two access points connected to the same switch and VLAN both advertise the SSID STAFF, and a laptop moves from one to the other without changing its IP address. Which term describes this arrangement?
options: IBSS
ESS
BSS
MBSS (mesh)
questions.explanation: Several BSSs with the same SSID joined by a wired **distribution system** form an **Extended Service Set**; the client roams between BSSIDs and keeps its Layer 3 identity.

whyWrong.0: An IBSS is ad hoc — clients talking directly with no AP at all.
whyWrong.2: A BSS is one AP's cell; here there are two cells cooperating.
whyWrong.3: A mesh BSS links APs over a wireless backhaul; these APs are both cabled to the switch.

questions.prompt: Every day around noon, 2.4 GHz clients near the break room lose throughput for a few minutes while 5 GHz clients in the same area are unaffected. What is the most likely cause?
options: A DFS radar event forcing the 2.4 GHz radio to change channel
Co-channel interference from a neighbouring 2.4 GHz cell
A hidden-node problem between clients on opposite sides of the cell
Non-Wi-Fi interference from a microwave oven in the break room
questions.explanation: A microwave oven radiates around 2.45 GHz while it runs, so the symptom is time-bound (lunch), place-bound (the break room) and band-bound (2.4 GHz only). Non-Wi-Fi sources never defer to CSMA/CA, so they simply corrupt frames.

whyWrong.0: DFS exists only in 5 GHz, and a radar move would affect the 5 GHz clients, not the 2.4 GHz ones.
whyWrong.1: A neighbouring cell is there all day; co-channel contention would not appear for a few minutes at noon.
whyWrong.2: Hidden-node collisions are not tied to a time of day or to one band.

questions.prompt: A company must remove a departing employee's Wi-Fi access without changing anything on the other 400 devices. Which WLAN security design supports this?
options: WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X and a RADIUS server
WPA3-Personal with a 63-character passphrase
WPA2-Personal with SSID broadcast disabled
WPA3-Personal, because SAE issues a key per user
questions.explanation: Enterprise mode authenticates each user individually through **802.1X/EAP** against a RADIUS (AAA) server, so disabling one account revokes one person. Any Personal mode shares one passphrase that would have to be changed everywhere.

whyWrong.1: A longer passphrase is still one passphrase known to everyone, including the leaver.
whyWrong.2: Hiding the SSID is not access control; the leaver already knows the name and the key.
whyWrong.3: SAE derives a fresh session key from the *shared* passphrase; it does not create per-user credentials.

Parabolic dish
Integrated AP omni
questions.explanation: A **parabolic dish** focuses the energy into a very narrow beam and so has the highest gain; that is what a long point-to-point link needs, with the two dishes aimed at each other.

whyWrong.0: A dipole radiates in every horizontal direction and wastes most of its energy away from the far building.
whyWrong.1: A patch covers a sector with moderate gain — good for a wall-mounted AP, too little for 3 km.
whyWrong.3: Integrated AP antennas are omnidirectional and designed for a room, not a link between buildings.

cards.front: Non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels in the North American plan?
cards.back: 1, 6 and 11 — their centres are 25 MHz apart (five channel numbers).

cards.front: 2.4 GHz channel spacing and transmission width?
cards.back: Centres 5 MHz apart; each transmission is 20 MHz wide (22 MHz for 802.11b DSSS), so neighbouring numbers overlap.

cards.front: 2.4 GHz frequency range and channel counts?
cards.back: 2.400–2.4835 GHz; 14 channels defined; 1–11 in the US, 1–13 in Europe, 14 is Japan and 802.11b only.

cards.front: How are 5 GHz 20 MHz channels numbered?
cards.back: Every 4th number: 36–64, 100–144, 149–165 (centre = 5000 + 5 × n MHz); none overlap; 25 in the US.

cards.front: DFS: which channels, and the three timers?
cards.back: 52–64 and 100–144; 60 s channel availability check, 10 s to leave on radar, 30 min non-occupancy.

cards.front: 6 GHz band facts?
cards.back: 5.925–7.125 GHz in the US (1,200 MHz, 59 × 20 MHz channels; EU only 500 MHz); 802.11ax/be only; WPA3 or OWE mandatory; no DFS.

cards.front: Channel widths by amendment?
cards.back: 20 MHz (a and g; 802.11b DSSS is 22 MHz), 40 MHz (n), 80 and 160 MHz (ac), 320 MHz (be, 6 GHz only). Wider = faster but fewer channels and less range.

cards.front: 0 dBm equals? Rule of 3s and 10s?
cards.back: 1 mW. +3 dB doubles, −3 dB halves, +10 dB is ×10. 20 dBm = 100 mW, 30 dBm = 1 W.

cards.front: dB vs dBm vs dBi?
cards.back: dB = a ratio between two powers; dBm = absolute power relative to 1 mW; dBi = antenna gain relative to an isotropic radiator.

cards.front: EIRP formula?
cards.back: Transmitter power (dBm) + antenna gain (dBi) − cable loss (dB). US 2.4 GHz limit 36 dBm; ETSI 20 dBm.

cards.front: SNR formula and Cisco's voice-cell targets?
cards.back: SNR = RSSI − noise floor, in dB. Voice: RSSI ≥ −67 dBm and SNR ≥ 25 dB.

cards.front: Wavelength at 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz?
cards.back: About 12.5 cm, 6 cm and 5 cm. Longer waves (lower frequency) penetrate and travel further.

cards.front: 802.11a, b and g — band and max rate?
cards.back: a: 5 GHz, 54 Mbps, OFDM. b: 2.4 GHz, 11 Mbps, DSSS. g: 2.4 GHz, 54 Mbps, OFDM.

cards.front: 802.11n, ac, ax, be — bands, max rate, Wi-Fi name?
cards.back: n: 2.4+5, 600 Mbps, Wi-Fi 4. ac: 5 only, 6.9 Gbps, Wi-Fi 5. ax: 2.4/5/6, 9.6 Gbps, Wi-Fi 6/6E. be: 2.4/5/6, 46 Gbps, Wi-Fi 7.

cards.front: SSID vs BSSID?
cards.back: SSID = the WLAN's name, up to 32 characters. BSSID = the 48-bit MAC address of one AP radio's cell.

cards.front: BSS, ESS and IBSS?
cards.back: BSS = one AP and its clients. ESS = several BSSs, same SSID, joined by a wired distribution system (roaming). IBSS = ad hoc, no AP.

cards.front: Co-channel vs adjacent-channel interference?
cards.back: Co-channel: same channel, both cells decode each other and share airtime — slow but clean. Adjacent: overlapping channels, frames corrupted — worse.

cards.front: Common non-Wi-Fi interferers?
cards.back: 2.4 GHz: microwave ovens (~2.45 GHz), Bluetooth, Zigbee, cordless phones, analogue cameras. 5 GHz: radar (triggers DFS).

cards.front: Cipher used by WEP, WPA, WPA2, WPA3?
cards.back: WEP: RC4 static key. WPA: TKIP (RC4, per-packet keys, Michael MIC). WPA2: AES-CCMP. WPA3: AES-CCMP, or GCMP-256 in Enterprise 192-bit mode.

cards.front: What did WPA3 change?
cards.back: SAE replaces the PSK exchange (forward secrecy, resists offline guessing); PMF (802.11w) mandatory; optional 192-bit Enterprise mode; Enhanced Open (OWE) alongside.

cards.front: Personal vs Enterprise mode?
cards.back: Personal: one passphrase (8–63 chars) via PSK or SAE. Enterprise: 802.1X/EAP with a RADIUS server (UDP 1812 auth, 1813 accounting); per-user credentials.

cards.front: Four antenna types and their patterns?
cards.back: Dipole/omni: doughnut, lowest gain. Patch: sector in front of a panel. Yagi: narrow beam. Parabolic dish: pencil beam, highest gain, point-to-point.

tickets.title: Strong signal, terrible throughput on the office 2.4 GHz WLAN
tickets.scenario: A small office runs one access point, OFFICE-AP, on 2.4 GHz channel 1. Since a new tenant moved in next door, users complain that Wi-Fi is painfully slow and file copies stall, even at desks right beside the AP. Nothing changed on the office side. You run two commands on a laptop sitting three metres from the AP.

tickets.question: What is the root cause of the poor throughput?
options: Weak signal: the AP is too far from the users and must be moved closer
Adjacent-channel interference: NEIGHBOUR-A on channel 3 overlaps channel 1 and corrupts the office cell's frames
Co-channel interference from NEIGHBOUR-B, which shares the office AP's channel
A DFS radar event has forced OFFICE-AP onto a congested channel
tickets.explanation: Signal is 88% (about −56 dBm), so RSSI is excellent — yet the link has dropped to MCS rates of 6.5 and 13 Mbps. A strong signal with a collapsing data rate means frames are being corrupted and retried, not lost to distance. The strongest neighbour (75%) sits on **channel 3**, which overlaps channel 1 almost entirely; neither cell can decode the other's preambles, so neither defers, and their transmissions collide as noise. That is adjacent-channel interference, and it arrived with the new tenant.
tickets.fix:
Move the office cell to the non-overlapping channel with the weakest neighbour — channel 11 (NEIGHBOUR-C at 20%) — and, if the client mix allows it, add a 5 GHz radio and steer clients there.

```text
OFFICE-AP → Wireless → Basic Wireless Settings → Standard Channel: 11 - 2.462GHz → Save Settings
```

On a Cisco Catalyst 9800 the same change for a lightweight AP is made from privileged EXEC:

```ios
WLC# ap name OFFICE-AP dot11 24ghz channel 11
```

On Monday, every laptop bought in the last two years connects normally, but a batch of older laptops sees the network, prompts for the passphrase, and then reports that it cannot connect. Retyping the passphrase does not help. You compare a failing laptop's adapter capabilities with what the network now advertises.

    802.11w Management Frame Protection supported : Yes

tickets.question: Why can the older laptops no longer connect?
options: The passphrase was changed during the migration and the old laptops still hold the previous one
Their 802.11ac adapters cannot associate with an 802.11ax access point
Their drivers support WPA2 but not WPA3 (SAE), so a WPA3-only WLAN rejects them
CCMP is not supported by the adapters, so the AP would have to fall back to TKIP
tickets.explanation: The WLAN now advertises **WPA3-Personal**, which authenticates with SAE. The failing laptop's driver lists WPA-Personal and WPA2-Personal but no WPA3 entry, so it cannot perform the SAE exchange; the passphrase is never even tested. The adapter supports CCMP and PMF, so the cipher and management-frame protection are not the problem — only the authentication method is.
tickets.fix:
Either update the adapter drivers on the older laptops to a version that lists WPA3-Personal, or run the WLAN in **WPA2/WPA3 transition mode** until they are replaced: enable both WPA2 and WPA3 on the WLAN with the PSK and SAE key-management methods, and set PMF to optional so that WPA2-only clients can still join.

```text
WLC → Configuration → Tags & Profiles → WLANs → CORP-WLAN → Security → Layer 2
  WPA2 + WPA3 enabled  ·  AKM: PSK and SAE  ·  PMF: Optional  ·  Cipher: AES (CCMP)
```

Transition mode is a stop-gap: a WPA2 client on the same SSID still uses the weaker PSK exchange, so plan to return to WPA3-only once the drivers are current.

questions.prompt: In a split-MAC architecture, which function stays in the lightweight AP rather than moving to the WLC?
options: Assigning channels and transmit power across all the APs
Holding the association state of clients as they roam
Running the 802.1X/EAP exchange with the RADIUS server
Sending beacons and acknowledging the frames clients send
questions.explanation: Split-MAC keeps the real-time 802.11 functions in the AP: beacons, probe responses, acknowledgements, RTS/CTS, power-save buffering and per-frame encryption all have timing requirements that cannot survive a round trip to the controller. Everything else moves to the WLC.

whyWrong.0: Channel and power assignment is Radio Resource Management, a controller function that needs a view of every AP.
whyWrong.1: Association and roaming state is held centrally so a client can move between APs without re-authenticating from scratch.
whyWrong.2: The controller runs the EAP exchange with the RADIUS server and pushes the resulting keys to the AP.

questions.prompt: A firewall separates a branch office from the data centre where the WLC lives. Which ports must be open for the branch's lightweight APs to join the controller and carry client traffic?
options: UDP 5246 and UDP 5247
UDP 12222 and UDP 12223
TCP 5246 and TCP 5247
UDP 1812 and UDP 1813
questions.explanation: CAPWAP uses two UDP tunnels to the controller's management address: control on **5246** (DTLS-encrypted) and data on **5247**. Both must pass any firewall between the AP and the WLC.

whyWrong.1: 12222 and 12223 belong to LWAPP, the Cisco protocol CAPWAP replaced.
whyWrong.2: CAPWAP runs over UDP, not TCP.
whyWrong.3: 1812 and 1813 are RADIUS authentication and accounting between the WLC and the AAA server, not between the AP and the WLC.

questions.prompt: A lightweight AP at 192.168.10.21 is joining this controller. To which address does its CAPWAP tunnel terminate, and why?

questions.explanation: APs build their CAPWAP tunnels to the interface that carries the AP-manager role. On modern AireOS controllers that is the management interface, shown here by `Ap Mgr Yes` next to `management`.

whyWrong.0: The virtual interface is an unroutable address used for DHCP relay, web-auth redirect and mobility; APs never tunnel to it.
whyWrong.1: A dynamic interface is where a WLAN's client traffic exits into its VLAN after decapsulation, not where the tunnel ends.
whyWrong.3: The service port is out-of-band management only and never carries AP or client traffic.

questions.prompt: Which two AP modes never serve wireless clients? (Choose two.)
options: Local
Monitor
FlexConnect
Rogue detector
Bridge
questions.explanation: **Monitor** mode turns the radios into full-time receivers for rogue detection, wIPS and location; **rogue detector** mode switches the radios off and listens on the wired side for MAC addresses seen behind rogue APs. Neither accepts client associations.

whyWrong.0: Local is the default client-serving mode; all client traffic is tunnelled to the WLC.
whyWrong.2: FlexConnect serves clients at a branch and can switch their traffic locally.
whyWrong.4: Bridge (mesh) APs serve clients on their access radio while using another radio for backhaul.

spec.caption: AP-BR1 is a lightweight AP in FlexConnect mode. Its own address is in VLAN 10; WLAN CORP is locally switched into VLAN 20 and WLAN GUEST into VLAN 30.

questions.prompt: Which configuration is correct for SW-BR Fa0/1, the port facing the FlexConnect AP in the exhibit?
options: switchport mode access · switchport access vlan 10 · spanning-tree portfast
switchport mode trunk · switchport trunk native vlan 10 · switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30
switchport mode trunk · switchport trunk native vlan 1 · switchport trunk allowed vlan 20,30
switchport mode access · switchport access vlan 20 · switchport voice vlan 30
questions.explanation: A FlexConnect AP that locally switches WLANs tags those client frames itself, so the port must be a trunk carrying VLANs 20 and 30. The AP's own CAPWAP traffic is sent untagged, so the native VLAN must be the AP's VLAN 10.

whyWrong.0: An access port is right for a local-mode AP, whose client traffic is inside CAPWAP; a locally switching FlexConnect AP needs the client VLANs on its own link.
whyWrong.2: With native VLAN 1 the AP's untagged CAPWAP packets land in VLAN 1, where the AP has no address, and the AP loses its controller.
whyWrong.3: A voice VLAN carries tagged frames from a phone; it does not deliver two WLAN VLANs plus the AP's management VLAN.

questions.prompt: A lightweight AP boots in a VLAN that contains no controller. Which DHCP option can hand it the management address of a WLC in another subnet?
options: Option 150, the Cisco TFTP server option
Option 66, the boot server host name
Option 6, the DNS server list
Option 43, the vendor-specific information option
questions.explanation: Cisco APs read WLC addresses from DHCP **option 43**, encoded as TLV `f1` (type 241), a length, and one or more 4-byte addresses — for example `f104.c0a8.0a05` for 192.168.10.5.

whyWrong.0: Option 150 tells Cisco IP phones where their TFTP server is; APs ignore it for discovery.
whyWrong.1: Option 66 names a boot/TFTP server for PXE-style clients, not a wireless controller.
whyWrong.2: Option 6 supplies DNS servers; that lets the AP resolve `CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER`, but it does not itself carry the controller address.

questions.prompt: A company with no existing controller opens a 12-person office with four APs. It wants centrally managed lightweight APs but will not buy a controller appliance, a Catalyst 9300 or a virtual-machine host. Which deployment model fits?
options: Centralized, with a Catalyst 9800-40 installed in a rack at the office
Mobility Express or EWC, with one of the APs acting as the controller
Cloud-based, with a Catalyst 9800-CL running in a private cloud
Embedded, with the controller software running on the office switch
questions.explanation: Mobility Express (Aironet) and the Embedded Wireless Controller on Catalyst 9100 APs run the WLC function on one of the APs, supporting up to about 100 APs and 2,000 clients — no appliance, switch-based controller or VM host required.

whyWrong.0: A 9800-40 is a dedicated appliance, which the company will not buy.
whyWrong.2: The 9800-CL is a virtual machine and needs a hypervisor host or cloud account, which was ruled out.
whyWrong.3: Embedded means the controller inside a Catalyst 9300/9400/9500 switch, which the company will not buy.

questions.prompt: A wireless user runs `ipconfig /all` and sees DHCP Server 192.0.2.1, although the company's real DHCP server is 10.10.10.10. What does 192.0.2.1 represent?
options: The WLC's virtual interface, which the controller presents to clients when it relays DHCP
The WLC's dynamic interface for the client's VLAN, which answers DHCP for that WLAN
A rogue DHCP server on the wireless segment that answered before the real server did
The lightweight AP's own management address, used to proxy DHCP for its clients
questions.explanation: When the controller relays (proxies) DHCP for wireless clients, the client sees the **virtual interface** address as its DHCP server. The address is deliberately unroutable — Cisco suggests `192.0.2.1`; older documentation used `1.1.1.1`.

whyWrong.1: The dynamic interface has a real address in the client VLAN (for example 192.168.20.5), and it forwards DHCP rather than answering as the server.
whyWrong.2: 192.0.2.1 is a documentation-range address chosen precisely because it cannot be a real host on the network.
whyWrong.3: A lightweight AP does not proxy DHCP; in local mode client frames go straight to the controller inside CAPWAP.

questions.prompt: A Cisco 5520 (AireOS) controller has LAG enabled and its two distribution ports are cabled to Gi1/0/1 and Gi1/0/2 on SW1. The exhibit shows the switch side. What is the root cause?
options: The switch ports are not configured as 802.1Q trunks, so the bundle cannot form
The controller has not been rebooted since LAG was enabled on its side
The switch is running LACP, but an AireOS LAG is static and needs channel-group mode on
The two ports were placed in different channel groups on the switch
questions.explanation: `Protocol LACP` with both members at `(I)` means the switch is sending LACP PDUs and hearing nothing back. An AireOS controller's LAG is a static bundle that never negotiates, so the switch must use `channel-group 1 mode on`.

whyWrong.0: Trunk mode does not affect whether a port-channel bundles; a mismatched trunk would show a different symptom.
whyWrong.1: A pending reboot on the controller would not make the switch report LACP as the protocol.
whyWrong.3: Both ports appear under group 1, so they are in the same channel group.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about CAPWAP between a lightweight AP and a WLC are true? (Choose two.)
options: The control tunnel is protected by DTLS by default
The data tunnel is protected by DTLS by default
The AP and the controller authenticate each other with digital certificates
Both tunnels run over TCP so that lost frames are retransmitted
The AP and the controller must share a VLAN for discovery to succeed
questions.explanation: CAPWAP control (UDP 5246) is always DTLS-encrypted, and the DTLS handshake authenticates both ends with X.509 certificates — the AP uses its manufacturer-installed certificate. The data tunnel (UDP 5247) is unencrypted unless data DTLS is explicitly enabled.

whyWrong.1: Data DTLS is optional and off by default; only the control tunnel is always encrypted.
whyWrong.3: CAPWAP uses UDP for both tunnels.
whyWrong.4: Discovery works across subnets via DHCP option 43, DNS or primed controller addresses; a shared VLAN is only the simplest case.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the service port on a Cisco wireless LAN controller is correct?
options: It is bundled into the LAG together with the distribution system ports
It terminates the CAPWAP control tunnels from the lightweight APs
It carries the client VLANs as an 802.1Q trunk toward the switch
It connects to an out-of-band access port on its own subnet
questions.explanation: The service port is for out-of-band management and recovery only. It cannot tag VLANs, so it plugs into an access port, and it must sit on a subnet different from the management interface.

whyWrong.0: Only the distribution system ports belong to the LAG; the service port is excluded.
whyWrong.1: CAPWAP terminates on the management (AP-manager) interface, which lives on the distribution ports.
whyWrong.2: Client VLANs leave through dynamic interfaces on the distribution ports, never through the service port.

questions.prompt: A lightweight AP in local mode will advertise three WLANs that the controller maps to VLANs 20, 30 and 40. The AP's own address is in VLAN 10. How should the AP's switchport be configured?
options: Trunk with VLANs 10, 20, 30 and 40 allowed and VLAN 10 native
Access port in VLAN 10 with PortFast enabled
Access port in VLAN 20 with VLAN 10 as the voice VLAN
Trunk with VLANs 20, 30 and 40 allowed and VLAN 1 native
questions.explanation: In local mode every client frame is carried inside CAPWAP to the controller, and the client VLANs are released on the WLC's trunk. The AP's port needs only the AP's own VLAN, so it is an access port in VLAN 10 — with PortFast, like any edge device.

whyWrong.0: Trunking the client VLANs to a local-mode AP is unnecessary; the AP never tags client frames.
whyWrong.2: The AP is not a phone, and its own traffic must be in VLAN 10, not VLAN 20.
whyWrong.3: A trunk with native VLAN 1 would put the AP's untagged CAPWAP traffic in the wrong VLAN and the AP would not join.

questions.prompt: The WLC's management interface is 10.10.0.5 in the data centre. The branch AP sits in 10.20.30.0/24 and the branch DHCP pool sets only a network, mask and default router. The AP repeats the exhibit every minute. What fixes it?
options: Add option 43 (or a DNS record for CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER) so the AP learns 10.10.0.5
Change the AP's switchport from access to trunk so it can reach the controller's VLAN
Configure a separate AP-manager interface on the controller for remote subnets
Enable LAG on the controller so the branch subnet is reachable through the bundle
questions.explanation: `Could not discover any MWAR` means the AP found no candidate controller. It has an address, but its subnet broadcast cannot reach 10.10.0.5 and nothing told it the address. DHCP option 43 (`f104.0a0a.0005`) or a DNS record for `CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER.<domain>` supplies it.

whyWrong.1: CAPWAP is routed IP; the AP does not need to be in the controller's VLAN, it needs to know the controller's address.
whyWrong.2: Modern controllers terminate CAPWAP on the management interface; a separate AP-manager does not help discovery.
whyWrong.3: LAG bundles the controller's distribution ports; it has nothing to do with reachability from a branch.

questions.prompt: An office runs Cisco Meraki access points managed from the Meraki dashboard. Where does a wireless user's traffic to a local file server go?
options: To the Meraki cloud, which inspects it and returns it to the LAN
Inside a CAPWAP tunnel to the nearest Meraki controller appliance
Straight from the AP onto the local VLAN mapped to that SSID
Through the AP's management tunnel to the dashboard and back
questions.explanation: Cloud-managed APs keep the data plane local: like an autonomous AP, a Meraki AP bridges each SSID onto a VLAN on its own uplink. Only configuration, monitoring and telemetry travel to the cloud.

whyWrong.0: Client data never crosses the Meraki cloud; the cloud is the management plane only.
whyWrong.1: There is no controller appliance in the cloud-managed model and no CAPWAP.
whyWrong.3: The management tunnel carries configuration and statistics, not user traffic.

questions.prompt: A wireless engineer needs a complete 802.11 frame capture from channel 36 delivered to a laptop running Wireshark. Which AP mode does the job?
options: Monitor
Rogue detector
SE-Connect
Sniffer
questions.explanation: **Sniffer** mode dedicates the AP to capturing every 802.11 frame on one channel and forwarding the frames (UDP 5555) to a host running Wireshark or OmniPeek.

whyWrong.0: Monitor mode scans all channels for rogues, intrusion and location data but does not stream a packet capture to a host.
whyWrong.1: Rogue detector mode switches the radios off and listens on the wire.
whyWrong.2: SE-Connect feeds a spectrum analyser with raw RF data, not decoded 802.11 frames.

cards.front: CAPWAP control tunnel — protocol and port?
cards.back: UDP 5246, always DTLS-encrypted; carries discovery, join, configuration and keepalives.

cards.front: CAPWAP data tunnel — protocol and port?
cards.back: UDP 5247; carries client 802.11 frames. Unencrypted unless data DTLS is enabled.

cards.front: Split-MAC: which functions stay in the lightweight AP?
cards.back: Real-time 802.11: beacons, probe responses, ACK/RTS/CTS, power-save buffering, per-frame encryption, QoS marking on the air.

cards.front: Split-MAC: which functions move to the WLC?
cards.back: Association/roaming, client authentication and key management, RRM (channel/power), security and QoS policy, bridging to the client VLAN.

cards.front: DHCP option that tells an AP its controller's address, and its encoding?
cards.back: Option 43: TLV `f1` (type 241) + length + 4 bytes per address, e.g. `option 43 hex f104.c0a8.0a05` = 192.168.10.5.

cards.front: DNS name a lightweight AP resolves to find a controller?
cards.back: `CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER.<local domain>` using the DNS server (option 6) and domain (option 15) from DHCP.

cards.front: Order in which an AP chooses among discovered controllers?
cards.back: Primary → secondary → tertiary (configured names) → master controller → least-loaded controller.

cards.front: Four Cisco WLC deployment models?
cards.back: Centralized/unified appliance; cloud-based (Catalyst 9800-CL VM); embedded (Catalyst 9300 switch); Mobility Express / EWC on an AP.

cards.front: Scale of Mobility Express / EWC-on-AP, and of an embedded (9300) controller?
cards.back: EWC-AP: about 100 APs / 2,000 clients. Embedded: about 200 APs / 4,000 clients.

cards.front: Cisco 'cloud-based' vs Meraki 'cloud-managed'?
cards.back: Cloud-based = the WLC itself is a VM in a cloud (9800-CL), APs still tunnel CAPWAP. Cloud-managed = no WLC; management in the Meraki dashboard, data switched locally by the AP.

cards.front: Switchport for a lightweight AP in local mode?
cards.back: Access port in the AP's management VLAN with PortFast; client VLANs are inside CAPWAP and appear on the WLC's trunk.

cards.front: Switchport for a FlexConnect AP with locally switched WLANs (or an autonomous/Meraki AP)?
cards.back: 802.1Q trunk: native VLAN = the AP's management VLAN (its own traffic is untagged), allowed = the client VLANs it switches.

cards.front: The four physical port types on a WLC?
cards.back: Distribution system ports (trunk/LAG), service port (out-of-band access port), redundancy port (HA SSO partner), console.

cards.front: The five logical interface types on an AireOS WLC?
cards.back: Management, AP-manager (legacy — management does it now), virtual, service-port, dynamic (one per client VLAN).

cards.front: Virtual interface — address and purpose?
cards.back: Unroutable address (`192.0.2.1`, formerly `1.1.1.1`); seen by clients as the DHCP relay and web-auth redirect; must match across a mobility group.

cards.front: Switch-side EtherChannel mode for an AireOS WLC LAG?
cards.back: `channel-group N mode on` — static; AireOS speaks no LACP or PAgP and supports one LAG containing all distribution ports. Catalyst 9800 also supports LACP/PAgP.

cards.front: AP mode that streams 802.11 frames to Wireshark?
cards.back: Sniffer mode — captures one channel and sends frames to a host on UDP 5555. Monitor mode scans all channels but sends no capture.

cards.front: AP mode that turns the radios off and needs a trunk port?
cards.back: Rogue detector — listens on the wired side for MACs of clients seen behind rogue APs, so it must see every VLAN.

cards.front: FlexConnect connected vs standalone — what survives if the WLC becomes unreachable?
cards.back: Standalone: locally switched, locally authenticated WLANs keep working and new clients can still join; centrally switched WLANs go down. A local-mode AP drops all its clients.

tickets.title: Branch APs never rejoin after a power cut
tickets.scenario: Last month the campus controller WLC1 was re-addressed: its management interface moved from `10.10.0.5` to `10.10.50.5` in a new VLAN. Campus APs, which sit in the controller's own VLAN, rejoined without help. Last night the BRANCH-1 office lost power. This morning its three APs have link lights and addresses, but no SSID is broadcast and none of them appears in `show ap summary` on WLC1. The branch router R-BR1 is the DHCP server for the AP VLAN.

tickets.question: Why do the branch APs fail to join, and what is the root cause?
options: The AP switchports are access ports; a remote AP needs a trunk to reach the controller's new VLAN
DHCP option 43 still encodes the old management address 10.10.0.5, so the APs send their discovery to a controller that no longer exists
The APs' DTLS certificates expired during the outage and the controller rejects their join requests
The controller's new subnet needs a dedicated AP-manager interface before APs outside its VLAN can join
tickets.explanation: The pool's `option 43 hex f104.0a0a.0005` decodes to `f1` (type 241), length `04`, address `0a.0a.00.05` = **10.10.0.5** — the controller's *old* address. The APs dutifully unicast discovery requests there and get nothing back (`Could not discover any MWAR`). Campus APs never noticed because they discover the controller by subnet broadcast. The WAN itself is fine: R-BR1 can ping the new management address. Before the power cut the branch APs were still running on primed controller information from their last successful join; the reboot sent them back through discovery with the stale option.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R-BR1(config)# ip dhcp pool AP-VLAN
R-BR1(dhcp-config)# option 43 hex f104.0a0a.3205
R-BR1(dhcp-config)# end
R-BR1# clear ip dhcp binding *
```
`0a0a3205` = 10.10.50.5. Power-cycle the APs (or wait for them to retry) and confirm with `show ap summary` on WLC1. Adding a DNS record `CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER.<domain>` → 10.10.50.5 gives a second discovery path for the future.

WLAN `CORP` stays centrally switched. Since the change, CORP clients work exactly as before, but GUEST clients associate and then sit at `169.254.x.x` — DHCP never answers. The branch switch SW-BR has VLAN 30 and a working DHCP scope for it.

tickets.question: Why do GUEST clients get no address while CORP clients are unaffected?
options: VLAN 30 has no dynamic interface on the controller, so the WLAN has nowhere to release its traffic
FlexConnect APs cannot locally switch a WLAN that uses a DHCP server on the branch LAN
Fa0/1 is an access port in VLAN 10, so the AP's VLAN-30-tagged GUEST frames are dropped; it needs a trunk with native VLAN 10 and VLAN 30 allowed
The controller's distribution trunk does not allow VLAN 30, so GUEST DHCP requests never reach the branch
tickets.explanation: With local switching enabled, AP-BR1 now bridges GUEST frames itself, tagged with VLAN 30, out of its own Ethernet port. That port is still the access port that was correct when the AP ran in local mode; an access port discards tagged frames for other VLANs, so the guests' DHCP DISCOVERs never reach SW-BR's VLAN 30. CORP still works because it is centrally switched — its frames travel inside CAPWAP, untagged, in VLAN 10, exactly as before. The fix keeps VLAN 10 as the native VLAN so the AP's untagged CAPWAP traffic still lands where the AP's address is.
tickets.fix:
```ios
SW-BR(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW-BR(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW-BR(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 10
SW-BR(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,30
SW-BR(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast trunk
SW-BR(config-if)# end
SW-BR# show interfaces fastethernet0/1 trunk
```
The AP stays joined throughout (its CAPWAP packets are untagged and still land in VLAN 10). Reconnect a guest client and confirm it receives a 10.20.31.x address from the branch scope.

questions.prompt: Employees were told that Staff-WLAN uses the passphrase `Harbour-Lights-77!`. Their laptops list the SSID but fail to connect, and no RADIUS server is defined on the controller. Which change makes the WLAN work as intended?
options: Enable WPA (SSN IE) so that older laptops can negotiate TKIP
Change the 802.11 authentication from Open System to Shared Key
Disable 802.1x and enable PSK under Auth Key Management, then set the key
Add the laptops' MAC addresses to a MAC filter on the WLAN
questions.explanation: The WLAN kept the AireOS default key management — **802.1x** — so the controller expects an EAP exchange with a RADIUS server that does not exist, and every PSK client fails at Layer 2. WPA2-Personal needs `PSK` enabled (and 802.1x disabled) plus the passphrase. The cipher (AES) is already correct.

whyWrong.0: WPA/TKIP is the deprecated 2003 generation; the problem is key management, not the cipher.
whyWrong.1: Shared Key is WEP-era 802.11 authentication; every WPA2 WLAN uses Open System at the 802.11 level.
whyWrong.3: MAC filtering is not authentication and would not supply the missing PSK exchange.

questions.prompt: Which encryption and integrity method does WPA2 use?
options: AES in counter mode with CBC-MAC (CCMP)
RC4 with per-packet key mixing and the Michael MIC (TKIP)
AES in Galois/Counter Mode with GMAC (GCMP)
RC4 with a static key and a CRC-32 integrity check value
questions.explanation: WPA2 implements IEEE 802.11i, whose cipher is **CCMP**: AES in counter mode for encryption and CBC-MAC for the message integrity check, both with a 128-bit key.

whyWrong.1: TKIP with Michael is the WPA (2003) method that kept RC4 for old hardware.
whyWrong.2: GCMP is the cipher Cisco associates with WPA3 (GCMP-256 is mandatory in WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode).
whyWrong.3: RC4 with a static key and CRC-32 is WEP.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe WPA3-Personal? (Choose two.)
options: It keeps the WPA2 PSK handshake but requires a 64-hex-digit key
It replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, defeating offline dictionary attacks
It re-introduces TKIP for compatibility with 802.11n clients
It makes Protected Management Frames mandatory
It authenticates each user with LEAP against a RADIUS server
questions.explanation: WPA3-Personal uses **SAE** (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals): each password guess costs a live exchange with the AP, so a captured handshake cannot be attacked offline, and every session gets a fresh PMK (forward secrecy). WPA3 also makes **PMF** (802.11w) mandatory, so deauthentication frames can no longer be spoofed.

whyWrong.0: SAE replaces the PSK-based handshake; the passphrase is still 8–63 ASCII characters.
whyWrong.2: TKIP is deprecated and forbidden with WPA3; WPA3-Personal uses CCMP-128.
whyWrong.4: LEAP is a deprecated Cisco EAP method; WPA3-Personal has no RADIUS server at all.

spec.title: WPA2 4-way handshake
spec.caption: Both sides derive the PTK from the PMK, the two nonces and the two MAC addresses.

questions.prompt: A laptop whose user mistyped the passphrase tries to join a WPA2-PSK WLAN. At which point does the join fail, and why?
options: Message 1 — the AP refuses to send the ANonce to an unknown client
Message 2 — the MIC computed from the wrong PMK does not verify at the AP
Message 3 — the client cannot decrypt the GTK and drops the association
802.11 association — the AP checks the passphrase before it accepts the client
questions.explanation: A wrong passphrase produces a wrong PMK and therefore a wrong PTK. The client's **message 2** carries a MIC computed with that PTK; the AP computes its own from the correct PMK, the MIC fails to verify, and the AP deauthenticates the client. That is why the SSID is visible and association succeeds but the client reports an incorrect password.

whyWrong.0: Message 1 is sent to any associated client; the AP has nothing to check yet.
whyWrong.2: The exchange never reaches message 3 — the AP stops after the failed MIC in message 2.
whyWrong.3: 802.11 authentication and association are Open System for every WPA generation; the passphrase is only proven in the handshake.

questions.prompt: Which pre-shared key does a wireless LAN controller reject for a WPA2-Personal WLAN?
options: A 63-character ASCII passphrase that contains spaces
A 64-digit hexadecimal string entered in HEX format
A 20-character ASCII passphrase of random symbols
A 7-character ASCII passphrase such as Lab2026
questions.explanation: An ASCII passphrase must be **8 to 63** printable characters; the HEX format is exactly **64** hexadecimal digits (the raw 256-bit PSK). Seven characters is below the minimum.

whyWrong.0: 63 is the maximum ASCII length and spaces are printable characters, so it is accepted.
whyWrong.1: 64 hex digits is precisely the raw-key format.
whyWrong.2: 20 characters is inside 8–63 and is a good length against offline guessing.

questions.prompt: In an 802.1X wireless deployment with a Cisco WLC and Cisco ISE, which device acts as the authenticator?
options: The wireless LAN controller, which relays EAP between the client and RADIUS
The RADIUS server, which validates the user's credentials
The client's supplicant software, which presents the credentials
The DHCP server, which admits the client once it has an address
questions.explanation: 802.1X defines three roles: the **supplicant** (client), the **authenticator** (the WLC — the AP only relays frames inside CAPWAP) and the **authentication server** (RADIUS, here ISE). The authenticator never checks credentials itself; it carries EAP in EAPoL on one side and in RADIUS on the other.

whyWrong.1: The RADIUS server is the authentication server, not the authenticator.
whyWrong.2: The client is the supplicant.
whyWrong.3: DHCP plays no role in 802.1X; addressing happens after authentication.

questions.prompt: A company requires an EAP method in which the client never sends a password and every device holds its own certificate. Which method meets the requirement?
options: PEAP with MS-CHAPv2 inside the TLS tunnel
EAP-FAST with a Protected Access Credential
EAP-TLS with client and server certificates
LEAP with mutual challenge-response
questions.explanation: **EAP-TLS** authenticates both sides with X.509 certificates; no password is ever exchanged. It is the strongest method and the only one permitted in WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode, at the cost of a PKI that issues a certificate to every client.

whyWrong.0: PEAP needs only a server certificate and passes a username/password (MS-CHAPv2) inside the tunnel.
whyWrong.1: EAP-FAST builds its tunnel with a PAC and normally carries a password inside it.
whyWrong.3: LEAP is a deprecated Cisco password method with no certificates and known offline attacks.

questions.prompt: A user reports "connected but no internet". Based on the controller output, where is the fault?
options: The passphrase is wrong — the 4-way handshake has not completed for this client
Layer 2 is complete; the client has no IP address yet — check DHCP in VLAN 10
The client is waiting for the web-authentication login page to load
The client has been excluded after repeated authentication failures
questions.explanation: `Policy Manager State DHCP_REQD` means the security phase finished (WPA2, PSK, CCMP are all shown as negotiated) and the controller is waiting for the client to obtain an IP address. The WLAN maps to interface `users` in VLAN 10, so the next checks are the DHCP scope for that subnet and whether VLAN 10 is allowed on the trunk to the controller.

whyWrong.0: A failed handshake never reaches DHCP_REQD; the client would show no negotiated cipher and would not stay Associated.
whyWrong.2: That would be `WEBAUTH_REQD`, and the client would already have an IP address.
whyWrong.3: An excluded client does not appear as Associated with a WLAN id.

questions.prompt: A new WLAN will carry Wi-Fi voice handsets. Which QoS profile should the WLAN use on an AireOS controller, and which default does it replace?
options: Gold, replacing the default Bronze
Silver, replacing the default Platinum
Bronze, replacing the default Gold
Platinum, replacing the default Silver
questions.explanation: The four profiles are **Platinum** (voice), **Gold** (video), **Silver** (best effort) and **Bronze** (background). A new WLAN defaults to Silver; a voice WLAN is set to Platinum so that voice-marked frames keep their priority.

whyWrong.0: Gold is the video profile, and Bronze is not the default.
whyWrong.1: Silver is the default, not the voice profile, and Platinum is not a default.
whyWrong.2: Bronze is the lowest (background) profile; Gold is not the default.

questions.prompt: Which two management access settings are enabled by default on a Cisco AireOS wireless LAN controller? (Choose two.)
options: HTTPS access to the GUI on TCP 443
Telnet access to the CLI on TCP 23
SSH access to the CLI on TCP 22
HTTP access to the GUI on TCP 80
Management sessions from wireless clients
questions.explanation: A fresh AireOS controller has **HTTPS** and **SSH** enabled and the clear-text protocols — HTTP and Telnet — disabled (`Management > HTTP-HTTPS` and `Management > Telnet-SSH`). Management via wireless clients is also disabled by default.

whyWrong.1: Telnet is disabled by default and should stay that way.
whyWrong.3: HTTP is disabled by default; only day-0 wizards and captive-portal redirects use it.
whyWrong.4: `Mgmt Via Wireless` is off by default so that a WLAN client cannot reach the controller GUI.

questions.prompt: On a Catalyst 9800, an engineer creates WLAN profile GUEST with WLAN ID 20, enables it and creates an enabled policy profile with the guest VLAN, yet no access point advertises the SSID. What is the most likely cause?
options: WLAN ID 20 exceeds the 16-WLAN limit and must be renumbered below 16
The WLAN must be bound to a dynamic interface before it is advertised
No policy tag maps the GUEST WLAN profile to the policy profile on those APs
The site tag assigned to the APs is missing an RF profile for 5 GHz
questions.explanation: On the 9800 a WLAN profile only reaches an AP through a **policy tag** that pairs it with a policy profile. WLAN IDs 1–16 are included in `default-policy-tag` automatically; ID 20 is not, so a tag entry (`wlan GUEST policy <profile>`) must be added to the tag the APs carry.

whyWrong.0: WLAN IDs above 16 are valid; they simply are not added to the default policy tag automatically.
whyWrong.1: Dynamic interfaces are an AireOS concept; the 9800 puts the VLAN in the policy profile.
whyWrong.3: RF profiles live in the RF tag, not the site tag, and they affect radio settings, not whether a WLAN is advertised.

questions.prompt: Sensors configured with the IoT-Sens passphrase cannot see the SSID at all. Which action fixes the problem?
options: Enable the WLAN with no shutdown — its status is DOWN
Change the key management from PSK to 802.1x to match CORP
Replace AES with TKIP because the sensors are 802.11g clients
Add the sensors' MAC addresses to a MAC filter on WLAN 2
questions.explanation: A WLAN with `Status DOWN` is configured but not advertised, so the very first step of joining — seeing the SSID — fails for every client. `no shutdown` under `wlan IOT` brings it up; its security (`[WPA2][PSK][AES]`) already matches sensors that use a passphrase.

whyWrong.1: 802.1x would require the sensors to run EAP against RADIUS; a passphrase is PSK.
whyWrong.2: TKIP is deprecated and the cipher has nothing to do with the SSID being invisible.
whyWrong.3: MAC filtering does not make a shut-down WLAN advertise.

questions.prompt: A café wants its open guest network to encrypt each client's traffic without asking anyone for a password. Which option provides that?
options: WPA2-Personal with the passphrase printed on every receipt
OWE (Enhanced Open), which derives keys with a Diffie-Hellman exchange
WebAuth passthrough with a pre-authentication ACL
Hiding the SSID and enabling MAC filtering on the WLAN
questions.explanation: **OWE** (Opportunistic Wireless Encryption, RFC 8110, branded Enhanced Open) runs a Diffie-Hellman exchange during association, derives a PMK and then uses the normal 4-way handshake and CCMP. Anyone can join, but each client's frames are encrypted with keys nobody else has.

whyWrong.0: A shared passphrase is still a password, and everyone who knows it shares the PMK.
whyWrong.2: WebAuth passthrough only gates access with an acceptance page; the data frames stay unencrypted.
whyWrong.3: Neither hiding the SSID nor MAC filtering encrypts anything.

questions.prompt: On an AireOS controller, which WLAN configuration page determines the VLAN that authenticated clients on that WLAN are placed in?
options: Security > Layer 2, through the Authentication Key Management selection
Advanced, through the Allow AAA Override checkbox
QoS, through the per-SSID bandwidth contract
General, through the Interface/Interface Group field
questions.explanation: The **General** tab's `Interface/Interface Group(G)` field binds the WLAN to a dynamic interface, and the dynamic interface carries the VLAN ID, address and DHCP server for the clients. That is the WLAN-to-VLAN mapping.

whyWrong.0: Key management decides PSK versus 802.1X; it has no VLAN.
whyWrong.1: AAA Override only lets a RADIUS server replace the WLAN's interface for individual users; the WLAN's own mapping is on the General tab.
whyWrong.2: Bandwidth contracts throttle traffic; they do not place clients in a VLAN.

questions.prompt: A 400-employee company runs its staff WLAN with WPA2-Personal. An employee who knew the passphrase has just left. Which statement best describes the situation and the fix?
options: Nothing is needed — the 4-way handshake derives a fresh key per session, so the old passphrase is useless
Every device must be re-keyed; moving to WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise lets one account be disabled instead
Enable client exclusion so the ex-employee's device is locked out after 60 seconds
Switch the PSK format from ASCII to HEX so the leaked passphrase no longer works
questions.explanation: With Personal mode everyone shares one secret, so revoking one person means changing the passphrase on every device. **Enterprise** (802.1X/EAP with RADIUS) gives each user their own credential, so leaving means disabling one account. Personal versus Enterprise is therefore a question of scale and accountability.

whyWrong.0: The PTK is per session, but anyone who knows the passphrase can still compute the PMK and join.
whyWrong.2: Client exclusion reacts to failed authentications; a device with the correct passphrase never fails.
whyWrong.3: The HEX format is the same PSK entered as 64 hex digits; the old passphrase still derives the same key.

cards.front: WEP: cipher and key?
cards.back: RC4 with a static 40- or 104-bit key and a 24-bit IV; CRC-32 integrity. Broken — never deploy it.

cards.front: WPA (2003): encryption and integrity method?
cards.back: TKIP (RC4 with per-packet key mixing and a 48-bit sequence counter) plus the Michael MIC. Deprecated.

cards.front: WPA2 (802.11i, 2004): encryption and integrity method?
cards.back: CCMP — AES-128 in counter mode for encryption, CBC-MAC for the MIC.

cards.front: WPA3: cipher, authentication and what became mandatory?
cards.back: Cisco pairs WPA3 with GCMP (AES-GCM + GMAC); in practice Personal runs CCMP-128 and 192-bit Enterprise needs GCMP-256 + EAP-TLS. SAE for Personal, 802.1X for Enterprise; PMF (802.11w) mandatory.

cards.front: Valid WPA/WPA2/WPA3 passphrase length?
cards.back: 8–63 printable ASCII characters, or exactly 64 hexadecimal digits (the raw 256-bit PSK).

cards.front: How is the PMK derived from a passphrase (Personal mode)?
cards.back: PBKDF2: 4096 rounds of HMAC-SHA1 over the passphrase with the SSID as salt → 256-bit PMK. The passphrase itself is never sent.

cards.front: 4-way handshake: input, outputs, and where a wrong passphrase fails?
cards.back: Input PMK; outputs PTK (unicast) and GTK (broadcast/multicast). A wrong passphrase fails at message 2 — the MIC does not verify.

cards.front: The three 802.1X roles on a WLAN?
cards.back: Supplicant = client; authenticator = WLC (AP relays); authentication server = RADIUS (ISE/NPS). EAPoL on the radio, RADIUS on the wire.

cards.front: Enterprise (802.1X/EAP) WLAN: which RADIUS ports?
cards.back: UDP 1812 authentication, UDP 1813 accounting. The WLC (the authenticator) wraps the client's EAP messages in RADIUS to reach the server.

cards.front: LEAP vs EAP-FAST vs PEAP vs EAP-TLS — one line each?
cards.back: LEAP: Cisco, password, no tunnel, deprecated. EAP-FAST: PAC builds the tunnel. PEAP: server certificate builds the tunnel, MS-CHAPv2 inside. EAP-TLS: certificates on both ends, no password.

cards.front: What does SAE add over the WPA2 PSK exchange?
cards.back: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (Dragonfly): every guess needs a live exchange (no offline dictionary attack) and each session's PMK is fresh (forward secrecy).

cards.front: PMF — standard, what it protects, WPA2 vs WPA3 status?
cards.back: 802.11w; adds a MIC to deauthentication, disassociation and robust action frames so they cannot be spoofed. Optional (Disabled/Optional/Required) in WPA2, mandatory in WPA3.

cards.front: OWE / Enhanced Open?
cards.back: Opportunistic Wireless Encryption: an open network that encrypts each client with a Diffie-Hellman-derived PMK — encryption without authentication.

cards.front: AireOS defaults on a newly created WLAN?
cards.back: Status disabled; Layer 2 WPA+WPA2 with WPA2 Policy, AES and key management 802.1X (untick it for PSK); interface management; QoS Silver.

cards.front: WLAN ID range on AireOS, and which IDs an AP advertises by default?
cards.back: IDs 1–512 per controller; APs in the default AP group advertise only IDs 1–16 (a radio can carry at most 16 SSIDs).

cards.front: The four WLC QoS profiles and the default?
cards.back: Platinum = voice, Gold = video, Silver = best effort (default), Bronze = background. A profile is a ceiling on 802.11e priority, not a promotion.

cards.front: Advanced-tab defaults: session timeout and client exclusion?
cards.back: Session Timeout 1800 s (re-authenticate every 30 min); Client Exclusion enabled, 60 s lockout after repeated failures.

cards.front: AireOS management protocol defaults?
cards.back: HTTPS (443) and SSH (22) enabled; HTTP (80) and Telnet (23) disabled; Management via Wireless disabled. Apply, then Save Configuration.

cards.front: Catalyst 9800: what do the policy, site and RF tags carry?
cards.back: Policy tag: WLAN profile ↔ policy profile (VLAN, switching, QoS, timers). Site tag: AP join profile and flex profile. RF tag: RF profiles per band. WLAN IDs 1–16 are auto-included in default-policy-tag.

cards.front: AireOS policy manager states DHCP_REQD, WEBAUTH_REQD and RUN mean?
cards.back: DHCP_REQD: Layer 2 done, waiting for an IP address. WEBAUTH_REQD: IP done, waiting for the web login. RUN: fully authenticated and forwarding.

tickets.title: Staff laptops see CCNA-Lab but every connection attempt fails
tickets.scenario: A new WLAN `CCNA-Lab` was created this morning on an AireOS controller for staff laptops, which are configured for **WPA2-Personal** with the passphrase `StudyLab-2026!`. Every laptop lists the SSID with full signal, prompts for the password, and then reports that it cannot connect. Some users now get no prompt at all for about a minute after several tries. The site has no RADIUS server. Nothing else on the network changed.

exhibits.title: WLC GUI — WLANs > Edit 'CCNA-USERS' > Security > AAA Servers
exhibits.text:
RADIUS Servers
  Authentication Servers   Server 1: None   Server 2: None   Server 3: None
  Accounting Servers       Server 1: None   Server 2: None   Server 3: None
Local EAP Authentication   [ ] Enabled

tickets.question: What is the root cause of the failed connections?
options: The WLAN's Layer 2 security is WPA with TKIP and the laptops only support AES
The WLAN kept the default 802.1X key management with no RADIUS server, so PSK clients fail at Layer 2
The clients are excluded because the 1800-second session timeout has expired
The WLAN is mapped to the users interface, so the 4-way handshake cannot complete
tickets.explanation: `show wlan 2` shows the cipher is fine (WPA2, AES) but **Auth Key Management is 802.1x Enabled / PSK Disabled** — the AireOS default on a new WLAN. The controller therefore starts an EAP exchange with every client and, with no RADIUS server on the AAA Servers tab, the exchange can never succeed. Laptops configured for a passphrase fail at Layer 2, and after repeated failures the client-exclusion policy locks them out for 60 s, which is the "no prompt for a minute" symptom in `show exclusionlist`.
tickets.fix:
In the GUI: `WLANs > Edit 'CCNA-USERS' > Security > Layer 2`, untick **802.1X**, tick **PSK**, PSK Format ASCII, enter `StudyLab-2026!`, Apply, then **Save Configuration**. The CLI equivalent (the WLAN must be disabled while its security changes):
```ios
(Cisco Controller) >config wlan disable 2
(Cisco Controller) >config wlan security wpa akm 802.1x disable 2
(Cisco Controller) >config wlan security wpa akm psk enable 2
(Cisco Controller) >config wlan security wpa akm psk set-key ascii StudyLab-2026! 2
(Cisco Controller) >config wlan enable 2
(Cisco Controller) >save config
```
`show wlan 2` now reports `PSK Enabled`; wait for the exclusion timers to expire (or clear the list) and the laptops join.

R1 has a DHCP pool for `10.0.10.0/24` and answers wired VLAN 10 clients correctly. This morning every wireless laptop connects, shows **Associated** on the controller, and then reports a `169.254.x.x` address and no connectivity. The passphrase has not changed.

tickets.question: Why do the wireless clients fail to obtain an address?
options: The dynamic interface users has the wrong DHCP server address configured
WPA2-PSK completed but the clients are being excluded for IP address theft
VLAN 10 is not allowed on the trunk to the controller, so DHCP requests for the users interface never reach R1
The WLAN needs DHCP Addr. Assignment Required enabled before clients can obtain addresses
tickets.explanation: The client record proves Layer 2 succeeded — WPA2, PSK and CCMP are negotiated and the state is **DHCP_REQD**, waiting for an address on interface `users` / VLAN 10. `show interfaces trunk` on the switch shows the trunk to the controller allows **only VLAN 99**, so the controller's VLAN-10-tagged DHCP Discover frames are dropped at Fa0/24 and never reach R1. Wired VLAN 10 clients work because they enter the switch on access ports, not through this trunk.
tickets.fix:
```ios
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 10
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```
`Vlans allowed on trunk` now reads `10,99`. Reconnect a laptop: `show client detail` moves to `Policy Manager State RUN` with a `10.0.10.x` address, and `show ip dhcp binding` on R1 lists the lease.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a Type 1 hypervisor?
options: It runs as an application on top of a general-purpose host operating system
It shares the host kernel with every guest instead of booting a separate OS
It runs directly on the server hardware and schedules the guest VMs itself
It is limited to Linux guests because it depends on kernel namespaces
questions.explanation: A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor such as ESXi, Hyper-V or KVM is installed directly on the hardware and is itself the layer that owns CPU, memory and NICs. Guests of any supported OS run on top of it.

whyWrong.0: Running on top of a host OS is the definition of a Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor such as VirtualBox.
whyWrong.1: Sharing the host kernel describes containers, not hypervisors; every VM has its own kernel.
whyWrong.3: Namespaces are a container mechanism; a Type 1 hypervisor runs Windows and Linux guests side by side.

questions.prompt: Which two products are Type 2 (hosted) hypervisors? (Choose two.)
options: VMware ESXi
Oracle VirtualBox
VMware Workstation Pro
Microsoft Hyper-V
KVM
questions.explanation: VirtualBox and VMware Workstation are installed as applications on Windows, macOS or Linux, so the host OS still owns the hardware. That makes them Type 2.

whyWrong.0: ESXi is installed directly on the server and is the classic Type 1 hypervisor.
whyWrong.3: Hyper-V is Type 1: once enabled, Windows itself runs as a privileged VM above the hypervisor.
whyWrong.4: KVM is a Linux kernel module that turns the kernel into a Type 1 hypervisor.

questions.prompt: A DevOps team must launch 40 copies of a small web service on one host in under a minute. Why do containers meet this requirement more easily than virtual machines?
options: Containers share the host kernel, so a start is a new process rather than an operating-system boot
Containers each carry a smaller guest kernel that boots faster than a full server operating system
Containers bypass the virtual switch and connect straight to the physical NIC, removing network delay
Containers are scheduled by the hypervisor with a higher priority than any virtual machine on the host
questions.explanation: A container is an isolated process on the host's existing kernel. Nothing boots, so start-up takes well under a second and the image is megabytes, not gigabytes. A VM has to boot a complete guest OS each time.

whyWrong.1: Containers have no kernel of their own at all; that is the whole point of sharing the host's.
whyWrong.2: Container networking goes through a Linux bridge (for example `docker0`); it is not faster at the NIC.
whyWrong.3: Containers are not managed by a hypervisor; a container engine such as Docker runs them.

questions.prompt: Gi1/0/10 is cabled to a single server. What is the most likely explanation for the output?
options: A switching loop is causing MAC addresses from other switches to be learned on Gi1/0/10
The server's NIC is spoofing addresses and the port should be err-disabled by port security
Gi1/0/10 is misconfigured as an access port and is learning frames from two VLANs
The server is a hypervisor host whose virtual switch sends frames from several VMs over one trunked uplink
questions.explanation: Five stable, distinct MAC addresses in the VMware OUI `0050.56` across two VLANs on one port is exactly what an ESXi host looks like: each vNIC has its own MAC and the vSwitch tags each VM's VLAN onto the uplink trunk.

whyWrong.0: A loop shows the same MAC flapping between ports and CPU spikes, not different stable MACs on one port.
whyWrong.1: Multiple legitimate MACs behind a hypervisor uplink are normal; port security with `maximum 1` would break it.
whyWrong.2: An access port learns MACs in one VLAN only; entries in VLANs 10 and 20 prove the port is trunking.

questions.prompt: An ESXi host has VMs in port groups tagged VLAN 10, 20 and 30, and the vSwitch adds the 802.1Q tag on its uplink. How should the Catalyst port facing the host be configured?
options: As an access port in VLAN 10, because a physical port can carry only one VLAN's untagged frames
As an 802.1Q trunk allowing VLANs 10, 20 and 30, with the native VLAN matching the vSwitch
As a routed port with an IP address in each of the three subnets so the VMs can reach their gateway
As an access port with `switchport voice vlan` so a second tagged VLAN is accepted from the host
questions.explanation: With virtual switch tagging the vSwitch sends tagged frames for each port group's VLAN, so the physical port must be a trunk that allows those VLANs. `switchport mode trunk` plus `switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30` and a matching native VLAN is the standard host-facing configuration.

whyWrong.0: An access port would drop the tagged VLAN 20 and 30 frames; the VMs in those port groups would lose connectivity.
whyWrong.2: A routed port has no VLANs at all; the VMs would have no Layer 2 path to their SVI gateways.
whyWrong.3: The voice VLAN feature accepts exactly one extra tagged VLAN for phones, not arbitrary VM VLANs.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about VRFs on a Cisco router are true? (Choose two.)
options: Each VRF has its own routing table and forwarding table, separate from the global table
A VRF encrypts traffic between its interfaces so other VRFs cannot read it
An interface can belong to several VRFs at once so tenants can share a link
The same IP subnet can be configured in two different VRFs on the same router
Routes in one VRF are reachable from the global table by default
questions.explanation: A VRF is an independent routing and forwarding context with its own set of interfaces. Because the tables never mix, overlapping prefixes are allowed across VRFs, which is why two tenants can both use 10.10.10.0/24 on one router.

whyWrong.1: VRFs provide logical separation only; encryption needs IPsec or another mechanism.
whyWrong.2: An interface belongs to exactly one VRF (or to the global table).
whyWrong.4: Nothing crosses between VRFs unless route leaking is deliberately configured.

questions.prompt: A host at 10.10.10.20 is connected behind Gi0/2, is powered on, and Gi0/2 is up/up. From R1's console, `ping 10.10.10.20` reports 0 percent success. Why?
options: Gi0/2 is administratively down because a VRF was applied after the address
Overlapping subnets on Gi0/1 and Gi0/2 make the router drop the echo requests
The ping is sourced from the global routing table, which has no route to 10.10.10.0/24
ICMP is not enabled inside the RED address family until `address-family ipv4` is added
questions.explanation: Plain `ping` consults the global routing table, and 10.10.10.0/24 exists only inside VRFs BLUE and RED. `ping vrf RED 10.10.10.20` would succeed. The failure says nothing about the link or the host.

whyWrong.0: The prompt states the interface is up/up; applying a VRF removes the address but does not shut the port.
whyWrong.1: Overlapping subnets are legal across VRFs; each table holds its own copy without conflict.
whyWrong.3: The address family is enabled under `vrf definition`, and it is a prerequisite for the VRF to hold IPv4 interfaces at all, not an ICMP switch.

exhibit.text:
