tickets.question: Why are there no OSPF routes although the neighbour is FULL?
options: The hello and dead timers are mismatched, so the adjacency is flapping between FULL and DOWN
R2's G0/0 is in the wrong area, so its LSAs are ignored by R1
The network types differ (point-to-point on R1, broadcast on R2): the timers match so FULL forms, but the link descriptions conflict and no routes are installed
An MTU mismatch on the transit is preventing the database exchange from completing
tickets.explanation: Both exhibits show hello 10 / dead 40 — the defaults for *both* broadcast and point-to-point — which is why the adjacency reaches FULL. But R1 describes the link as a point-to-point connection while R2 describes a transit network with a DR; the two router LSAs cannot be matched in the SPF calculation and neither side installs the other's prefixes. A wrong area would prevent the adjacency entirely, and an MTU mismatch would leave it stuck in EXSTART/EXCHANGE, not FULL.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
```
The adjacency re-forms and `show ip route ospf` on R1 shows `O 10.255.20.0/24` and the `O*E2` default within a few seconds.

tickets.question: What is the root cause?
options: R2's NAT ACL no longer includes 10.10.20.0/24, so guest packets leave untranslated and never return
The GUEST DHCP pool was deleted, so guests are running on stale leases that R1 no longer recognises
Line 35 denies every guest packet to any destination that was not permitted above it, dropping gateway pings and Internet traffic at R1
VLAN 20 has been removed from the trunk between SW1 and R1, so guest frames never reach G0/0.20
tickets.explanation: Sequence 35 sits above the intended denies and the final permit, and its destination is `any`, so once a guest packet fails lines 10–30 it is dropped — including pings to the guest's own gateway. Its 116 matches are the dropped traffic; line 70's counter has stopped moving. DHCP still works because line 10 comes first, which is why the laptops keep valid addresses. R2 shows only a staff translation because guest packets never leave R1, so NAT is not the cause; and a trunk fault would also break DHCP.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R1(config)# ip access-list extended GUEST-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# no 35
```
Re-run the acceptance tests: guest → gateway and Internet succeed, guest → staff still fails on line 40, staff → guest still succeeds via line 20.

tickets.question: What is the root cause?
options: `default-information originate` requires the `always` keyword before OSPF will advertise any default route
R2's static default route to 203.0.113.2 was deleted, so R2 has no default of its own and stops originating one into OSPF
The OSPF adjacency between R1 and R2 has dropped, so R1 lost every route learned from HQ
R2's ISP-facing interface is down, which withdraws the connected 203.0.113.0/24 and the default with it
tickets.explanation: R2's own table has no gateway of last resort, and `default-information originate` without `always` only advertises a default that R2 actually has. The OSPF configuration is intact, the neighbour is FULL (branch users still reach 10.255.20.10), and the ISP link is up because R2 pings 203.0.113.2. Adding `always` would make R1 send Internet traffic to R2, which would then drop it — the real fix is to restore the static.

```ios
R2(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.2
```

questions.prompt: PC-A can ping every other host in its office but nothing beyond it. Based on the exhibit, what is the problem?
options: 172.16.47.250 is the broadcast address of the subnet and cannot be assigned to a host
The default gateway 172.16.48.1 is outside the PC's subnet, which spans 172.16.44.0 to 172.16.47.255
A 172.16.0.0 address is Class B, so the mask must be 255.255.0.0 for the gateway to be reachable
The mask 255.255.252.0 leaves too few host bits, so the PC's address collides with the gateway
questions.explanation: A /22 has a block size of 4 in the third octet, so 172.16.47.250 sits in 172.16.44.0/22, whose range is 172.16.44.1–172.16.47.254. The gateway 172.16.48.1 belongs to the next block; a host's default gateway must be on its own subnet, so local traffic works and everything else fails.

whyWrong.0: The broadcast address of 172.16.44.0/22 is 172.16.47.255; .250 is a valid host.
whyWrong.2: Classful masks have not applied since CIDR; a /22 on a 172.16 address is normal.
whyWrong.3: A /22 leaves 10 host bits, 1022 usable addresses; there is no collision.

spec.title: VLAN 10 · Rapid PVST+
spec.caption: SW1 is the root. All ports have default cost and priority.

questions.prompt: Which port is SW3's root port for VLAN 10, and why?
options: Fa0/24, because it connects directly to the root bridge
Gi0/1, because SW2 has a lower MAC address than SW1
Gi0/1, because the two-hop gigabit path costs 8 against 19 on the direct link
Fa0/24, because the lower port number wins when SW3 receives two BPDUs
questions.explanation: The root port is the port with the lowest total cost to the root, adding the cost of each receiving interface. Through SW2 the cost is 4 + 4 = 8; the direct FastEthernet link costs 19. Hop count never enters the calculation.

whyWrong.0: A direct link is not preferred; only cost matters, and 19 loses to 8.
whyWrong.1: Sender bridge ID is only a tie-breaker when costs are equal, and SW1's ID is lower anyway.
whyWrong.3: Port number is the last tie-breaker and only applies between equal-cost paths from the same neighbour.

questions.prompt: R1 and R2 share an Ethernet segment and both run OSPF, but `show ip ospf neighbor` on R1 is empty. Which two parameters must match on the two interfaces for the adjacency to form? (Choose two.)
options: The OSPF process ID
The hello and dead timers
The router ID
The area ID
The interface bandwidth
questions.explanation: OSPF neighbours must agree on the area, the subnet, the hello and dead intervals, the network type and any authentication before they exchange hellos successfully. Timers and area are carried in every hello, and a hello whose values do not match is discarded.

whyWrong.0: The process ID is locally significant and never leaves the router.
whyWrong.2: Router IDs must be **unique**; identical router IDs prevent the adjacency.
whyWrong.4: Bandwidth affects the cost of the route, not whether the neighbour forms.

questions.prompt: A packet arrives at R1 destined for 10.1.3.77. Which next hop does R1 use?
options: 10.9.9.2, because the static route has the lowest administrative distance
10.9.9.1, because the OSPF route to 10.1.0.0/16 has the lowest metric
203.0.113.1, because the default route is the gateway of last resort
10.9.9.3, because 10.1.3.64/26 is the longest prefix that matches
questions.explanation: Forwarding always picks the longest matching prefix first. 10.1.3.77 falls inside 10.1.3.64/26 (64–127), which is more specific than /24 or /16, so the OSPF route via 10.9.9.3 wins regardless of its higher AD and metric.

whyWrong.0: AD only decides between sources offering the **same** prefix; /24 and /26 are different prefixes.
whyWrong.1: Metric is compared only among routes to the same prefix from the same protocol; /16 is the least specific match here.
whyWrong.2: The default route is used only when no other prefix matches.

questions.prompt: Hosts in 10.10.10.0/24 cannot reach the internet and `show ip nat translations` stays empty. What is wrong?
options: GigabitEthernet0/0/1 is missing `ip nat outside`, so no translation is ever built
The ACL must be an extended list so that PAT can track the TCP and UDP port numbers
The `overload` keyword requires a NAT pool rather than an interface address
Access-list 1 must permit 203.0.113.0 0.0.0.3 so the outside address can be used
questions.explanation: NAT translates only packets that cross from an `ip nat inside` interface to an `ip nat outside` interface. With no outside interface defined, packets leave untranslated with private sources and the translation table never populates.

whyWrong.1: A standard ACL identifying the inside source addresses is the normal and sufficient form.
whyWrong.2: `interface ... overload` is exactly how PAT to the interface address is configured.
whyWrong.3: The ACL selects inside addresses to translate; the outside address never appears in it.

questions.prompt: An extended ACL on R1 must block Telnet from 192.168.10.0/24 to the host 10.0.0.5 and permit all other traffic. Which two lines, entered in this order, achieve it? (Choose two.)
options: `access-list 110 permit ip any any`
`access-list 110 permit tcp any any eq 23`
questions.explanation: Extended ACLs use numbers 100–199 (or 2000–2699), wildcard masks, a protocol, and an optional port on the destination. The deny must come first, and because every ACL ends with an implicit deny, an explicit `permit ip any any` is needed to let everything else through.

whyWrong.1: 255.255.255.0 is read as a wildcard: it ignores the first three octets and requires a last octet of 0, so it matches any x.x.x.0 source, not the subnet.
whyWrong.3: A standard ACL cannot match a port, and this line would block every packet from the subnet.
whyWrong.4: This permits Telnet from other sources but leaves all non-Telnet traffic to the implicit deny.

questions.prompt: PCs in VLAN 20 receive no DHCP address. The DHCP server is 10.0.0.10 on a different subnet, reachable through R1, whose subinterface G0/0.20 (10.20.0.1/24) is the VLAN 20 gateway. Which configuration fixes it?
options: `ip helper-address 10.0.0.10` on R1's subinterface G0/0.20
`ip forward-protocol udp bootps` in R1's global configuration
`ip helper-address 10.0.0.10` on the R1 interface that faces the server
`ip dhcp pool VLAN20` on R1 with `default-router 10.20.0.1`
questions.explanation: A router does not forward broadcasts, so the DISCOVER from VLAN 20 dies at the gateway. `ip helper-address` on the interface that **receives** the broadcast turns it into a unicast to the server, with `giaddr` set to 10.20.0.1 so the server picks the right pool.

whyWrong.1: `ip forward-protocol` only selects which UDP ports a helper address relays; with no helper address configured, nothing is relayed.
whyWrong.2: The helper goes on the client-facing interface, where the broadcast arrives, not the server-facing one.
whyWrong.3: That makes R1 a DHCP server, which is not what the design with an existing server asks for.

whyWrong.1: Critical is 2 and warning is 4; the sequence is emergency, alert, critical, error, warning, notification, informational, debugging.
whyWrong.3: Sequence numbers, when enabled, appear at the start of the line, before the timestamp.

options: HSRP always keeps the router with the lower IP address as the active router
Priority 150 is invalid, because HSRP priorities run only from 0 to 100
R1 must also be at priority 150, and the tie went to R1 because of its IP address
R2 is not configured to preempt, so R1, which came up first, keeps the active role
questions.explanation: HSRP does not preempt by default. Once a router is active it stays active until it fails, whatever priority a later router announces. The empty `P` column on R2 confirms `standby 1 preempt` is missing; adding it makes R2 take over immediately.

whyWrong.0: IP address is only the tie-breaker when priorities are equal, and the **higher** address wins.
whyWrong.1: HSRP priority ranges from 0 to 255; 150 is common and valid.
whyWrong.2: Nothing in the exhibit shows equal priorities, and a tie would favour the higher IP, which is not what decides here.

questions.prompt: Three APs in an open-plan office use the 2.4 GHz band on channels 1, 4 and 8. Users under the middle AP report slow, erratic throughput. Which change is correct?
options: Move all three APs to channel 6 so that they share one clean channel
Use channels 1, 6 and 11 — the only three 2.4 GHz channels that do not overlap
Bond channels 4 and 8 into one 40 MHz channel to give the middle AP more capacity
Raise the transmit power on the middle AP so its signal overrides the neighbours
questions.explanation: 2.4 GHz channels are 5 MHz apart but about 22 MHz wide, so channel 4 overlaps with both 1 and 8; the middle AP suffers adjacent-channel interference from both neighbours. Only channels 1, 6 and 11 are spaced far enough apart not to overlap.

whyWrong.0: Three APs on one channel contend for the same airtime — co-channel interference.
whyWrong.2: Channel bonding on 2.4 GHz consumes most of the band and worsens overlap; it is a 5 GHz practice.
whyWrong.3: More power increases the interference the middle AP causes without removing what it receives.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about port security on a Catalyst switch are true? (Choose two.)
options: Sticky MAC learning is enabled as soon as `switchport port-security` is entered
The default maximum is one secure MAC address per port
The port may be left in `dynamic auto` mode before port security is enabled
In `restrict` mode a violation shuts the port down but does not log it
The default violation action is `shutdown`, which puts the port into err-disabled
questions.explanation: Enabling port security with no other keywords allows exactly one MAC address and, on a violation, shuts the port into the err-disabled state. Everything else — sticky learning, higher maximums, `protect` or `restrict` — has to be configured explicitly.

whyWrong.0: Sticky learning needs `switchport port-security mac-address sticky`.
whyWrong.2: Port security is rejected on a dynamic port; the port must be a static access or trunk port.
whyWrong.3: `restrict` keeps the port up, drops the offending frames and increments the violation counter with a log message.

exhibit.title: GET /api/v1/device/SW1 — response body

questions.prompt: In this JSON response, which statement about the data types is correct?
options: `uptime` is a string, because JSON requires numbers to be quoted
`managed` is a string that happens to contain the word true
`interfaces` is an object with two key-value pairs inside it
`interfaces` is an array containing two objects
questions.explanation: Square brackets denote a JSON array (an ordered list) and curly braces denote an object (key-value pairs). `interfaces` is therefore an array whose two elements are objects. `86400` without quotes is a number and `true` without quotes is a boolean.

whyWrong.0: Numbers are written unquoted; `"86400"` would be a string, `86400` is a number.
whyWrong.1: Unquoted `true` is the boolean value, not the string `"true"`.
whyWrong.2: Objects use braces; the outer brackets make `interfaces` an array.

questions.prompt: An interface with MAC address 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E builds its link-local address with modified EUI-64. Which address results?
options: FE80::21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
FE80::1A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
FE80::1A2B:3CFF:FE4D:5E00
questions.explanation: Modified EUI-64 splits the MAC in half, inserts `FFFE` between the halves (00:1A:2B **FF:FE** 3C:4D:5E) and flips the seventh bit of the first byte, turning `00` into `02`. Leading zeros drop, so `021A` becomes `21A` under the link-local prefix FE80::/10.

whyWrong.1: The seventh bit was not flipped; `00` must become `02`.
whyWrong.2: The `FFFE` padding is missing, so the interface ID is only 48 bits.
whyWrong.3: `FFFE` was inserted in the wrong place and the bit was not flipped.

questions.prompt: An administrator wants every configuration command that engineers type on the routers to be individually authorised by a central server. Which protocol and port does the router use toward that server?
options: RADIUS on UDP 1812, because it authorises commands on a per-user basis
TACACS+ on TCP 49, because it separates authorisation from authentication
RADIUS on UDP 1645, the port reserved for authorisation traffic
TACACS+ on UDP 49, because it encrypts the entire packet body
questions.explanation: TACACS+ runs over TCP port 49, encrypts the whole packet body and keeps authentication, authorisation and accounting as separate exchanges, which is what allows per-command authorisation. RADIUS bundles authentication and authorisation together and cannot authorise individual commands.

whyWrong.0: RADIUS (UDP 1812/1813) merges authentication and authorisation; it has no per-command authorisation.
whyWrong.2: 1645 is the legacy RADIUS authentication port, and the protocol still cannot authorise commands.
whyWrong.3: The encryption claim is right but TACACS+ uses TCP, not UDP.

questions.prompt: SW1's ports Gi0/1 and Gi0/2 are configured with `channel-group 1 mode passive`. Which mode on SW2's matching ports brings the LACP port channel up?
options: passive, so that both ends negotiate symmetrically
desirable, the mode that actively initiates the bundle
active, because at least one LACP end must initiate
auto, which responds to whichever protocol arrives
questions.explanation: LACP forms a bundle when at least one side is `active`; `passive` only answers. `passive`–`passive` never negotiates. `desirable` and `auto` are PAgP keywords and cannot pair with LACP at all.

whyWrong.0: Two passive ends both wait to be asked and the channel never forms.
whyWrong.1: `desirable` is PAgP; PAgP and LACP do not interoperate.
whyWrong.3: `auto` is PAgP's passive mode and will not answer LACP PDUs.

tickets.title: OSPF over the new WAN link never reaches FULL
tickets.scenario: Branch router R1 was moved to a new provider Ethernet service toward HQ router R2. The engineer who cut it over added `ip mtu 1400` on R1's G0/0/1 "to avoid fragmentation over the provider's tunnel". Since then the HQ routes have vanished from R1 and users cannot reach anything at HQ. Both routers can ping each other across the /30.

exhibits.title: R1# show ip ospf neighbor
exhibits.text:
Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   EXSTART/DR      00:00:36    10.255.12.2     GigabitEthernet0/0/1

exhibits.title: R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0/1 | include MTU
exhibits.text: MTU is 1400 bytes

exhibits.title: R2# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0/0 | include MTU
exhibits.text: MTU is 1500 bytes

tickets.question: What is the root cause of the stuck adjacency?
options: The hello and dead timers differ between R1 and R2, so the adjacency resets every 40 seconds
R2 is the DR and R1 has priority 1, so R1 cannot exchange its database with a DR
The IP MTU differs (1400 versus 1500), so the database description exchange in ExStart never completes
The two routers have the same router ID, so each one rejects the other's database description packets
tickets.explanation: The routers already see each other's hellos — that is what got them past Init and 2-Way — so timers and areas match. ExStart is where the neighbours compare the MTU carried in the database description packet; a mismatch makes the router with the smaller MTU refuse the exchange, and the state oscillates between EXSTART and EXCHANGE forever. The two `MTU is` lines prove it.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0/1
R1(config-if)# no ip mtu 1400
```
If the provider really needs 1400 bytes, set the same `ip mtu 1400` on R2's G0/0/0 instead, or add `ip ospf mtu-ignore` on both ends.

tickets.title: Nobody in VLAN 20 gets an address since DHCP snooping was switched on
tickets.scenario: Access switch SW2 serves VLAN 20 phones and PCs. Yesterday DHCP snooping was enabled on SW2 after a rogue DHCP server incident. Since then every client that renews or reboots ends up with a 169.254.x.x address; hosts with static addresses are unaffected. The company DHCP server sits in the data centre and is reached through SW2's uplink Gi0/1 to the distribution switch.

exhibits.title: SW2# show ip dhcp snooping
exhibits.text:
Switch DHCP snooping is enabled
DHCP snooping is configured on following VLANs:
20
DHCP snooping is operational on following VLANs:
20
DHCP snooping is configured on the following L3 Interfaces:

Insertion of option 82 is enabled
   circuit-id default format: vlan-mod-port
   remote-id: 0c22.bbbb.bbbb (MAC)
Option 82 on untrusted port is not allowed
Verification of hwaddr field is enabled
Interface                  Trusted    Allow option    Rate limit (pps)
-----------------------    -------    ------------    ----------------

exhibits.title: SW2# show logging | include DHCP_SNOOPING
exhibits.text: %DHCP_SNOOPING-5-DHCP_SNOOPING_UNTRUSTED_PORT: DHCP_SNOOPING drop message on untrusted port, message type: DHCPOFFER, MAC sa: 0011.2233.4455

tickets.question: What is the root cause?
options: Option 82 insertion is enabled, so the DHCP server rejects the relayed DISCOVER messages
The uplink Gi0/1 toward the DHCP server is untrusted, so the switch drops every OFFER that arrives on it
DHCP snooping is enabled globally but not on VLAN 20, so the switch cannot build a binding table
The access ports are untrusted, so the clients' DISCOVER broadcasts are dropped before leaving the switch
tickets.explanation: DHCP snooping treats every port as untrusted until told otherwise, and server messages (OFFER, ACK, NAK) arriving on an untrusted port are dropped — exactly what the log line reports for a DHCPOFFER. The interface table at the bottom of `show ip dhcp snooping` is empty, so no port has been trusted, including the uplink through which the legitimate server answers.
tickets.fix:
```ios
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
```
Optionally add `ip dhcp snooping limit rate 10` on the access ports and leave them untrusted — that is the point of the feature.
